Lactose intolerance can increase the risk of osteoporosis, primarily through an indirect pathway: when lactose-intolerant individuals avoid dairy products, they often reduce their calcium intake, which can weaken bones over time [d1][d3][d6]. According to NHS Inform, difficulty obtaining adequate vitamins and minerals may put lactose-intolerant people at increased risk of osteopenia and osteoporosis [d1]. MedicineNet states directly that "the important long-term health consequence of lactose intolerance is calcium deficiency which leads to osteoporosis," and that vitamin D deficiency may compound the bone disease [d5]. A peer-reviewed source on ScienceDirect confirms that lactose intolerance has been associated with osteoporosis development and is a predictor of fracture, with the connection attributed to reduced calcium intake from avoidance of milk products [d3]. However, a PMC meta-analysis notes that lactose intolerance is "probably not a direct factor of osteoporosis development"; rather, it is the failure to replace dairy with other calcium-rich foods that may cause decreased bone mineral density [d7]. The NIH recommends that lactose-intolerant individuals consume fortified foods or supplements to meet calcium requirements and reduce this risk [d2].
